_about: D52's strike cases, frozen. Source: D52 (nearest $10; an exact tie rounds away from the previous close, so below the close rounds down and above rounds up; the 7th strike, the rounded close itself, ties up; rounded once from Pyth's integer and exponent, never after first rounding to cents), D6 and D49 (the plus and minus 3, 6 and 9 percent ladder and the $10 step, config/program-devnet.json), and the spec's META and AAPL examples. A close is Pyth's integer price and exponent (price x 10^exponent dollars); strikes are cents. A frozen golden file: changing it is a logged decision.

cases.about: D52: a $500.00 close. -3% is exactly $485.00 and rounds down to 480 (below the close); +3% is exactly $515.00 and rounds up to 520; -9% is $455.00 and rounds down to 450; +9% is $545.00 and rounds up to 550.

D52: a $499.995 close, which Pyth can report with five decimals. Rounded once from the exact price: +3% is $514.99485 (510), +9% is $544.99455 (540). Rounding the close to $500.00 first would give 520 and 550 (the $500.00 case), so the order of the roundings changes two strikes.
The spec's META example: previous close $680 gives 620, 640, 660, 680, 700, 720, 740.
The spec's AAPL example: previous close $230 gives seven ladder points that deduplicate to 5 strikes: 210, 220, 230, 240, 250.
D52: the rounded previous close itself, the 7th strike, rounds a tie up ($685.00 gives $690). Other points: 705.55 to 710, 664.45 to 660, 726.10 to 730, 643.90 to 640, 746.65 to 750, 623.35 to 620.
The same $500.00 close written with exponent -2 (Pyth's exponent can differ): the strikes must not depend on the exponent.
The same $500.00 close written with exponent -8: the strikes must not depend on the exponent.
